notes:
I now have substantial material. Let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from across the traditions represented.

---

## Mark 15:25–47 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### v. 25: “It was the third hour when they crucified Him.”

- **The time reference.** Mark gives the time as the third hour — about 9:00 a.m. by Jewish reckoning (counting from sunrise, roughly 6:00 a.m.). This is the only Gospel that specifies the hour of crucifixion. Gill notes that this was the time of the daily morning sacrifice at the temple and the hour when the Sanhedrin normally convened — a grim irony, since the priests ought to have been at the temple. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **The apparent discrepancy with John.** John 19:14 says it was “about the sixth hour” (noon) when Pilate handed Jesus over. Bible.org explains the standard resolution: the Synoptic Gospels consistently use Jewish time (counting from 6:00 a.m.), while John often uses Roman time (counting from midnight), making “the sixth hour” in John roughly 6:00 a.m. — the time of Pilate’s verdict, not the crucifixion itself. Others suggest Mark means the close of the third hour, and that Jesus was crucified and hung between roughly 9:00 a.m. and noon. (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-15)

- **Calvin’s explanation (from the CCEL study page).** Calvin notes that the day was divided into four parts, each named from its first hour. “The third hour” covered the period from about 9:00 a.m. to noon, and Mark means Jesus was crucified toward the close of that period — not contradictory to John’s “sixth hour.” He adds that Christ probably did not hang on the cross longer than three hours. (https://www.ccel.org/study/Mark_15:25-37)

- **The Light of Israel Bible Commentary** adds that penitential prayers at the third, sixth, and ninth hours continued in the church for centuries, as recorded in the Apostolic Constitutions (AD 375–380). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/mark-15.html)

---

### v. 26: “And the charge inscribed against Him read: THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

- **The “titulus.”** This was the written notice of the crime, a Roman custom designed to publicise the reason for execution. Gill calls it “the superscription of his accusation” or “the cause of his death,” written over His head on the cross. John 19:20 adds that it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)** notes that Pilate meant this charge as both a final mockery of Jesus and a final mockery of the Jewish leaders — yet it proclaimed the truth. Jesus was indeed the King of the Jews, though not in the political sense Pilate assumed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that the tablet with the inscription would have been carried before Jesus in the procession to Golgotha, then affixed to the cross — all part of Rome’s public “advertisement” of the execution. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/15.htm)

---

### v. 27: “Along with Jesus, they crucified two robbers, one on His right and one on His left.”

- **For greater reproach.** Gill says Jesus was placed between two thieves “as if he had been one of them, and a principal among them” — designed to humiliate Him utterly. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **David Guzik** notes that these were likely not mere petty thieves but “robbers” (Greek *lēstēs*), a word also used for insurrectionists — men like Barabbas. Jesus, the innocent, was placed in the place of the guilty. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

---

### v. 28: [KJV only; not in the oldest manuscripts] “And the scripture was fulfilled, which saith, And he was numbered with the transgressors.”

- **A scribal addition.** Most modern translations omit this verse or bracket it. Bible.org notes that some manuscripts include wording similar to Luke 22:37. Gill, writing before modern textual criticism, treats it as genuine and identifies it as a quotation of Isaiah 53:12: Christ “was no transgressor of the law of God himself … yet he was treated by the justice of God as if he had been a transgressor.” The earliest and best manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) lack the verse. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

---

### vv. 29–30: “And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads and saying, ‘Aha! You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, come down from the cross and save Yourself!’”

- **Fulfilment of Psalm 22.** Both Gill and the Pulpit Commentary note that the wagging of heads and mocking directly echo Psalm 22:7–8: “All who see me mock me; they hurl insults, shaking their heads.” The mockers twisted Jesus’ words about the temple (Mark 14:58; John 2:19), which He spoke of His body, into a taunt. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/15.htm)

- **Peake’s Commentary** observes a profound irony: “Unconsciously, they disclose His glory.” The taunts reveal who He truly is even as they mock Him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html)

- **David Guzik** notes that the mockers were probably local Jerusalemites — most Galilee pilgrims were still in the countryside — and they echoed the false charges from the trial. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

---

### vv. 31–32a: “In the same way, the chief priests and scribes mocked Him among themselves, saying, ‘He saved others, but He cannot save Himself! Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!’”

- **Unwitting testimony.** The religious leaders spoke a deeper truth than they knew. Guzik quotes General Booth: “They would have believed in Him had He come down; we believe in Him because He stayed up.” Jesus could not save Himself *and* save others; it was precisely by refusing to come down that He accomplished salvation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **Gill** notes the mockery among themselves (the Syriac reads “laughed at one another”), having gained their point and satiated their revenge. They demanded a sign — “come down … that we may see and believe” — yet when Jesus gave the greatest sign (the resurrection), they still refused to believe. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **Peake’s Commentary:** “He saved others” is an unintentional confession of Jesus’ miraculous power; “Himself He cannot save” is the deepest theological truth of the atonement. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html)

---

### v. 32b: “And even those who were crucified with Him berated Him.”

- **Both robbers initially reviled Him.** Mark states that both criminals insulted Jesus. Luke 23:39–43 records that one later repented. Gill notes that Matthew 27:44 also says both initially reviled Him. There is no contradiction: both began by mocking, and one was later converted through witnessing Jesus’ gracious response. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

---

### v. 33: “From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land.”

- **Supernatural darkness, not a natural eclipse.** Guzik (Enduring Word) argues strongly that this could not be a solar eclipse because Passover falls at a full moon — an eclipse of the sun is astronomically impossible at full moon. This was a supernatural sign, a mark of creation’s agony at the Creator’s suffering. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **A sign of divine judgment.** The Gospel Coalition article on penal substitution notes that this was “not the regular darkness of nighttime, but a unique darkness, a divine darkness” — signifying that Jesus was dying under the curse. It echoes the plague of darkness in Egypt (Exodus 10) and the prophetic words of Amos 8:9: “I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight.” (https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/article/how-marks-account-of-the-crucifixion-helps-us-understand-penal-substitution/)

- **Modern critical view (Peake’s Commentary).** Peake suggests the darkness may not be historical but rather “suggested by such a passage as Amos 8:9 or by the belief that nature mourns heroes” (citing Plutarch). He notes that the RV margin rejects “earth” in favour of “land.” This reflects a more sceptical approach to the supernatural. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html)

- **Bible.org** simply notes the three-hour span: noon to 3:00 p.m. The time markers in Mark (third hour, sixth hour, ninth hour) correspond to the times of the daily temple sacrifices and traditional prayer times. (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-15)

---

### v. 34: “At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, ‘Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?’ which means, ‘My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?’”

- **The Cry of Dereliction — the traditional Protestant understanding.** David Guzik writes: “When Jesus cried ‘My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?’ He experienced real separation from the Father’s fellowship and bore the actual outpouring of the Father’s wrath upon Him for our sin.” This is the heart of penal substitutionary atonement: Jesus, who had never known a moment’s separation from the Father, now bore the full weight of divine wrath so that believers would never need to. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **DesiringGod (John Piper).** In his article “Why Have You Forsaken Me?”, Piper explains that Jesus quotes Psalm 22:1 not merely as a pointer to the psalm but as a real experience of God-forsakenness. The Father turned His face away because Jesus was bearing sin. The cry is “the measure of the distance between feeling and fact” — Jesus *felt* forsaken because He truly was under the curse, yet He was still the beloved Son. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/why-have-you-forsaken-me)

- **Peake’s Commentary** offers a more agnostic reading, quoting Glover: “Strange to think that is the cry of the feeling of Jesus. One is almost tempted to say that there, as in a supreme instance, is measured the distance between feeling and fact. So He felt; and yet mankind has been of another mind, that there, more than in all else that He was or did, there was God.” Peake says “we do not know the exact significance of this strange and seemingly desolate cry.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html)

- **A note on the language.** Gill notes that “Eli, Eli” (Matthew) and “Eloi, Eloi” (Mark) are both Hebrew/Aramaic forms of “My God,” and both appear in Psalm 22:1, from which the whole cry is taken. Mark uses the Aramaic form, which explains why bystanders thought He was calling Elijah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **Ligonier (R.C. Sproul).** Sproul emphasises that what was happening at the cross was “the most momentous cosmic event imaginable” — an atonement “by which the wrath and justice of God were satisfied by a substitute.” Bystanders could not have understood this without the later instruction of the Epistles and the illumination of the Holy Spirit. The cry reveals the reality of the wrath-bearing. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-crucifixion)

---

### vv. 35–36: “When some of those standing nearby heard this, they said, ‘Behold, He is calling Elijah.’ And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine … saying, ‘Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to take Him down.’”

- **Misunderstanding or mockery?** Gill suggests the bystanders either ignorantly or wilfully mistook “Eloi” for “Elias” (Elijah). Peake’s Commentary notes that in Hebrew “Eli, Eli” could more easily be misunderstood as calling Elijah, but Mark has the Aramaic “Eloi,” making the confusion stranger — perhaps the bystanders were Greek-speaking and simply misheard. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html)

- **The sour wine.** Gill identifies this as the fulfilment of Psalm 69:21: “They gave me vinegar to drink.” The Pulpit Commentary distinguishes two occasions when drink was offered: (1) before crucifixion — wine mingled with myrrh, a narcotic, which Jesus refused (v. 23); (2) here, near death — sour wine (*oxos*), the cheap wine-vinegar soldiers drank, offered in response to “I thirst” (John 19:28). Jesus accepted this second drink. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/15.htm)

- **The taunt about Elijah.** Some see this as continuing mockery; others (Peake’s) suggest it could be curiosity or even a flicker of expectation. In Jewish tradition, Elijah was expected to come to the aid of the righteous. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html)

---

### v. 37: “But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last.”

- **A loud cry, not a whimper.** Gill notes this was a second loud cry — the first being “Eloi, Eloi…” and this second being the words recorded in Luke 23:46 (“Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit”) and John 19:30 (“It is finished”). The loud cry is remarkable because crucifixion victims typically died of asphyxiation and could barely whisper. Jesus’ strong cry demonstrated that He voluntarily gave up His life. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **Guzik** adds that Jesus “breathed His last” — literally “expired” (*exepneusen*) — indicating an active, voluntary yielding of His spirit, not merely succumbing to physical trauma. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

---

### v. 38: “And the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.”

- **God tore it.** The direction — from top to bottom — shows God Himself acted. DesiringGod’s article explains that the veil separated the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies, the place of God’s immediate presence, into which only the high priest could enter once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Its tearing signifies that through Jesus’ death, access to God is now open to all. Hebrews 10:19–22 makes this explicit: “we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way opened for us through the curtain, that is, his body.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-veil-was-torn-in-two)

- **Which curtain?** Ligonier (R.C. Sproul) notes that Mark does not specify whether this was the inner veil (separating the Holy of Holies from the Holy Place) or the outer veil (separating the Court of Women from the Court of Israel). There are good arguments for both. Either way, the message is the same: Jesus’ death removes barriers to God’s presence. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/centurions-confession)

- **DesiringGod** notes a literary connection unique to Mark: at Jesus’ baptism, the heavens were “torn” (*schizō* — Mark 1:10); at His death, the temple veil is “torn” (*schizō* — Mark 15:38). The same verb links these two events. The tearing of the heavens revealed Jesus’ identity as God’s Son at His baptism; the tearing of the veil does the same at His death, leading directly to the centurion’s confession. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-veil-was-torn-in-two)

- **The Pulpit Commentary** adds: “The veil signified that heaven was closed to all, until Christ by his death rent this veil in twain, and laid open the way.” It notes that this happened at the very moment of Jesus’ death, and that the veil was enormous — according to Jewish tradition, it was as thick as a hand’s breadth and required many priests to move it. Its tearing was a physically impossible event without divine intervention. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/15.htm)

---

### v. 39: “When the centurion standing there in front of Jesus saw how He had breathed His last, he said, ‘Truly this man was the Son of God!’”

- **A Gentile’s confession.** Ligonier (R.C. Sproul) calls the centurion “the first to realize that something of cosmic significance was happening that afternoon outside Jerusalem.” As a Roman officer who had overseen many crucifixions, he knew a routine execution from something extraordinary. The manner of Jesus’ death — the loud cry, the sudden expiration, the darkness, the earthquake (Matthew 27:54) — convinced him that this was no ordinary man. Sproul says: “the centurion was among those most unlikely to recognize Jesus and yet God revealed Christ to him.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/centurions-confession)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** sees the centurion as a picture of all who come to Jesus through the cross — fulfilling Jesus’ promise in John 12:32: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to Myself.” The first convert at the cross was a pagan Roman soldier. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **“Son of God” — what did he mean?** The Pulpit Commentary observes that the centurion may not have understood the full theological meaning of “Son of God” as Christians do. Yet he had observed Jesus through those weary hours, had seen the meekness, dignity, and supernatural signs, and could come to no other conclusion than that this man was in very deed God’s Son. Tradition (recorded by Chrysostom) identifies this centurion as Longinus, who later became a Christian herald and was martyred in Cappadocia. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/15.htm)

- **Baptist/Reformed nuance.** The centurion’s confession is a model of saving faith: it came not through intellectual argument but through beholding the crucified Christ. John Piper (DesiringGod) and Sproul (Ligonier) both stress that this was a work of divine revelation — God opened the centurion’s eyes. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-crucifixion)

---

### vv. 40–41: “And there were also women watching from a distance. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. These women had followed Jesus and ministered to Him while He was in Galilee …”

- **Faithful women.** The Pulpit Commentary highlights the faith and love of these women, who “in the very presence of the enemies of Christ dared to stand by his cross, and shrank not from testifying their piety and devotion.” John says they stood near the cross; Matthew and Mark say “from a distance.” The Pulpit harmonises: they “came as near as they could,” perhaps sometimes nearer and sometimes further as the soldiers permitted. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/15.htm)

- **Who they were.** Mary Magdalene (out of whom Jesus had cast seven demons — Mark 16:9); Mary the mother of James the younger (*ho mikros*) and Joses — possibly the same as “Mary the wife of Clopas” (John 19:25); and Salome — identified in Matthew 27:56 as the mother of the sons of Zebedee (James and John). These women had followed Jesus from Galilee and supported His ministry financially and practically. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/15.htm)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** observes: “Faithful women were last at the cross and first at the tomb.” While the male disciples (except John) had fled, these women stayed. Mary Magdalene especially “would have to be counted as a disciple par excellence.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **The Light of Israel Bible Commentary** adds: “We cannot discount the great importance of women in the gospel. In fact, Mary Magdalene would have to be counted as a disciple par excellence since she did what the other disciples, with exception of John, were unwilling or unable to do.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/mark-15.html)

---

### v. 42: “Now it was already evening. Since it was Preparation Day (that is, the day before the Sabbath) …”

- **Urgency.** The Pulpit Commentary explains: the Sabbath began at 6:00 p.m. Friday evening. “Our Lord must be buried before six o’clock.” Mark alone mentions that evening had already come — the timeline was extremely tight. The Jewish law (Deuteronomy 21:22–23) required that a hanged criminal be buried the same day, and this being the eve of the Sabbath made it doubly urgent. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/15.htm)

- **Bible.org** notes that Mark is the only Gospel to specify “when evening had already come.” Jewish reckoning had two “evenings”: (1) 3:00–6:00 p.m. (the time of the evening sacrifice), and (2) after 6:00 p.m. (the start of the new day). The context implies it was after 3:00 p.m. but before 6:00 p.m. (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-15)

- **Preparation Day.** Gill explains this was Friday, the day when Jews prepared food and everything needed for the Sabbath, on which no work could be done. This confirms that Jesus was crucified on a Friday. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

---

### v. 43: “Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God, boldly went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus.”

- **A secret disciple no longer.** Guzik notes that Joseph was “apparently silent when the council sentenced Jesus to death (Mark 15:1).” Now, after Jesus’ death, he “took courage” and acted openly. His boldness contrasts with his earlier secrecy. The Light of Israel Commentary says: “It appears here that the secret disciple, Joseph of Arimathea, was now no longer secret.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/mark-15.html)

- **“A prominent Council member.”** Gill describes him as “an honourable counsellor” — possibly a priest serving on the Sanhedrin’s priestly bench. He was “waiting for the kingdom of God,” meaning he was a devout Jew who looked for the Messiah. The Pulpit Commentary calls him a man “of a good aspect, well dressed, and that behaved well and honourably in his office.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **Unusual request.** Normally the bodies of crucified criminals were left on the crosses to be devoured by birds and wild animals (as the Roman historian Suetonius attests). The Light of Israel Commentary notes that because of Jewish sensibilities and the approaching festival, the Romans permitted burial. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/mark-15.html)

- **R.C. Sproul (Reformed)** emphasises that this act was courageous: Joseph risked his reputation and position. He says the burial marks the turning point from Jesus’ humiliation to His exaltation — “The beginning, the point of transition from suffering to exaltation, is found in His burial” because it fulfils Isaiah 53:9: “He was assigned a grave … with the rich in His death.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-burial-jesus)

---

### vv. 44–45: “Pilate was surprised to hear that Jesus was already dead, so he summoned the centurion … When Pilate had confirmed it with the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph.”

- **Why Pilate marvelled.** Gill explains: “death, by crucifixion, was a slow lingering death; persons that were in their full strength hung a great while before they expired; and the two thieves, which were crucified with Christ, were not dead when he was.” Typically crucifixion took days. Jesus died in about six hours. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **Confirmed dead.** Guzik notes: “Pilate personally investigated the matter of Jesus’ death and found reliable eyewitness testimony from the centurion, who had witnessed perhaps hundreds of crucifixions and knew if a man was dead or not.” He quotes Cole: “A Roman sergeant had seen too many deaths to be in any uncertainty about such a fact.” The Light of Israel Commentary adds that we have “the expert opinion of the Roman centurion who watched him die,” plus the soldiers who did not break Jesus’ legs because He was already dead (John 19:33), and the soldier who pierced His side (John 19:34). This rules out any “swoon theory.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/mark-15.html)

- **Bible.org** notes that the Greek word used for “body” in v. 45 is *ptōma* (corpse), not *sōma* (living body). Mark is unambiguous: Jesus was dead. (https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-15)

- **R.C. Sproul** highlights that Pilate’s verification with the centurion — the very officer who had just confessed Jesus as Son of God — gives the burial account legal weight: the death is doubly attested by Roman officialdom. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-burial-jesus)

---

### v. 46: “So Joseph bought a linen cloth, took down the body of Jesus, wrapped it in the cloth, and placed it in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance to the tomb.”

- **Joseph’s own tomb.** Matthew 27:60 specifies it was Joseph’s own new tomb. Guzik calls it “a borrowed tomb.” The Pulpit Commentary notes the fulfilment of Isaiah 53:9: “They made His grave with the wicked … but with the rich at His death.” Jesus, who owned nothing in life, was buried in a rich man’s tomb. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **Hasty but honourable.** Gill notes Joseph “bought fine linen” — an expensive fabric. He and Nicodemus (John 19:39–40, who brought about 75 pounds of myrrh and aloes) performed a hurried but dignified burial. Because the Sabbath was approaching (at sundown), there was no time for the full traditional preparation of the body. The women noted this and planned to return after the Sabbath (Mark 16:1). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **A rock-hewn tomb.** Typical of wealthy Jewish burials of the period, the tomb was cut out of solid rock, with a stone (likely a large disc-shaped stone rolled in a groove) sealing the entrance. Guzik notes that this was protection “against wild beasts and thieves” (citing Menzies). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **Sproul (Reformed)** frames the burial as the beginning of Jesus’ exaltation. He argues that while the resurrection is the zenith of exaltation, “the beginning, the point of transition from suffering to exaltation, is found in His burial” — because burial with the rich fulfils Isaiah’s prophecy that the Suffering Servant would be vindicated. Jesus’ humiliated body received an honourable burial, signalling that the humiliation phase had ended. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-burial-jesus)

- **Defilement for the sake of love.** The Light of Israel Bible Commentary points out that Joseph, by touching a dead body, made himself ceremonially unclean and unable to participate in the Passover/Sabbath observances. He sacrificed his religious standing to honour Jesus. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/mark-15.html)

---

### v. 47: “Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed.”

- **Witnesses.** Guzik (Enduring Word) explains that these women observed the burial carefully: “They wanted to make sure that Jesus was properly prepared for burial.” More importantly, their presence provided the necessary two witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15) to confirm where Jesus was buried — so that no one could later claim the disciples went to the wrong tomb on resurrection morning. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/)

- **Who is “Mary the mother of Joseph”?** Dummelow’s Commentary raises an interesting textual question. In Greek, she is called “Mary of Joses” (or “Mary of Joseph”). Dummelow argues she is probably not the same as “Mary the mother of James and Joses” (v. 40), since the evangelist would not describe the same woman differently in consecutive verses. He suggests she may be “Mary the daughter of Joses” — possibly the daughter or wife of Joseph of Arimathea, or of some other unknown Joses. This represents a minority textual view. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/mark-15.html)

- **Most traditional commentators** (Gill, Pulpit) identify her as the same Mary who was the mother of James the Less and Joses (i.e., “the other Mary” of Matthew 27:61), and the two descriptions are complementary rather than contradictory. Gill reads “Mary the mother of Joses” and the Vulgate and Ethiopic support “Joseph” here. The Pulpit Commentary equates her with “Mary the wife of Clopas, or Alphaeus, and mother of James the less and of Joses, called brethren of our Lord.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-15.html)

- **Light of Israel Commentary** adds: “faithful women were last at the cross and first at the tomb of Jesus.” These women could not anoint the body now (the Sabbath was about to begin), but they marked the spot so they could return. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/loi/mark-15.html)

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Distinctives

### Reformed / Reformed Baptist (Ligonier, DesiringGod, The Gospel Coalition)
- Emphasise **penal substitutionary atonement** in v. 34: Jesus bore the Father’s wrath as a substitute. The darkness (v. 33) is a sign of divine curse. The veil (v. 38) is torn by God Himself, signifying the new covenant and direct access to God.
- The centurion’s confession (v. 39) demonstrates God’s sovereign, gracious revelation to an unlikely Gentile.
- R.C. Sproul uniquely identifies the **burial** (not the resurrection) as the turning point from humiliation to exaltation, because it fulfils Isaiah 53:9.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (EnduringWord / David Guzik)
- Strong emphasis on the **physical reality** of Jesus’ suffering — detailed medical descriptions of crucifixion.
- The **supernatural darkness** is stressed as a sign that could not be natural (not an eclipse).
- The centurion’s confession fulfils the “draw all people” promise of John 12:32 — a missional, Spirit-empowered reading.
- Women’s faithfulness is highlighted as exemplary discipleship.

### Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon echoes in EnduringWord)
- Gill provides detailed **rabbinic background** (e.g., the Sanhedrin’s sitting times, the Jewish custom of drugged wine).
- Emphasis on **fulfilled prophecy** at every point (Psalm 22, Isaiah 53, Psalm 69).
- Spurgeon’s emphasis (quoted by Guzik) is on the emotional and devotional — “Was there ever grief like his?”

### Older Anglican / Conservative (Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott)
- Careful **harmonisation of Gospel accounts** (e.g., the two occasions of drink offered, the women’s distance from the cross).
- Detailed **historical and geographical notes** (location of Pilate’s residence, site of Golgotha, Roman trial procedures).
- The tradition that the centurion was **Longinus**, later a martyr, is recorded.

### Modern Critical Scholarship (Peake’s Commentary)
- Raises the possibility that the **darkness** was suggested by Amos 8:9 or by the ancient belief that nature mourns heroes — not necessarily historical.
- The cry of dereliction is presented as **ambiguous**: “We do not know the exact significance.”
- The **time discrepancy** between Mark (third hour, 9 a.m.) and John (sixth hour, ~noon) is noted as “cannot easily be harmonised,” reflecting a willingness to accept Gospel differences without forced harmonisation.

### Evangelical (Bible.org)
- Provides **text-critical notes** (e.g., v. 28 absent from best manuscripts; the Greek variants in v. 8).
- Explains the **time discrepancy** through the Jewish vs. Roman time distinction, and notes John sometimes uses both.
- Emphasises that the Gospels are **theological documents**, not strict western chronological histories — “The Gospel writers, under inspiration, had the freedom to select, adapt, and rearrange.”
